label: text
text: Professor Maximlhen Langsner, a Pole who has devoted his life to the study of telepathy ("thought feeling," as he prefers to call it and hypniotism is at present in Hongkong in the course of a world tour.

label: text
text: The practice adopted by Prof. Langsner is to make a prolonged stay in each country, for the purpose of carrying out observations which will enable him to perfect his art. He realises that this cannot be accomplished in the space of a few weeks such as might enable a novelist to write a passably good novel with certain local colour. His study of the psychology of the peoples of the various countries included in his itinerary is extended over a considerable period. He has been on his travels for some years and intends to devote another two or three to life in China and Japan. The countries he has visited in the course of the present tour are Greece, Egypt, Persia, India or Indo-China.

label: text
text: Prof. Tangsner has given demonstrations in telepathy in some of the places he has visited. Such demonstrations are not, however, the main purpose of his visit. He does not wish to pose as a charlatan and it is only if there is a genuine desire among the people with whom he is staying for a demonstration in telepathy and hypnotism that he would give them such an opportunity of appreciating its possibilities. He emphasises that his feats are not illusions, in fact he prefers to have a sceptical audience.

label: text
text: If it should be practicable for a local demonstration to be given, Hongkong people will have the opportunity of witnessing the remarkable powers which Prof. Langsner undoubtedly possesses. Ino Indo-China, according to the Press, "this claim to read the mind of another was genuinely proved. It was the most convincing demonstration of telepathy yet given to a theatre audience."

label: text
text:
Similar appreciation is reported from the other places he has visited, glowing accounts being given of his almost incredible demonstrations, sceptics who challenged him being reported as entirely convinced of the genuineness of his claims and subsequently becoming his friends and advocates. In Calcutta, where he was challenged to make a long "distance" telepathic communication, he detailed what was happening in certain streets in Paris and London, events which were confirmed by the manager of Reuters in Calcutta.
In Cairo, before a packed audience five lions placed in an arena were mesmerised and, in the words of one of the newspapers, "became as quiet as the docile cats of Angora." Whilst in Persia, the Professor was awarded the order of the "Sun and Lion" by the Sha and presented with a pair of Persian carpets. Another test to which he was subjected in India China was to drive a car blindfolded for a long distance, the occupants of the car being French officials.
Prof. Langsner is a gifted linguist, speaking no less than six-

label: text
text: Prof. Langsner is a gifted linguist, speaking no less than sixteen languages. He was a personal friend of the late Enrico Caruso who was also a student of the occult. Writing to him on one occasion the great singer said "You hypnotise the world with your eyes. I hypnotise the world with my voice. We are both hypnotisers."

label: text
text: The end of the term at Victoria British School (East Point) was made the occasion of an open day, parents and friends visiting the premises this morning and taking advantage of the opportunity of seeing the work done by the young pupils during the term and of observing the excellent system on which the school is run.

label: text
text: The basis on which the methods of instruction are founded is that the pupils should actively co-operate with the teachers as much as possible. In this particular, the representation of events which are under study by means of tableaux constructed by the pupils themselves is worthy of mention. The pupils are encouraged to cut out from picture books the several ingredients to the scenes, the idea being that, pictorially represented, they convey a deeper meaning than mere words can do. The story of "Hiawatha" is under study at the moment and the students have helped to construct the actual scenes, with wigwam, Indians and all complete.

label: text
text: Specimens of the work of the scholars in needlework, designing, stencilling, etc., were on display, also some of the examination papers. These were the object of much interest by the parents and friends who were welcomed by Mrs. E. M. Clark, Headmistress, and conducted over the premises by the staff and pupils.

label: text
text: Mrs. Clark, in welcoming those present, thanked the parents for their co-operation in the conduct of the school and the training of the children and expressed the hope that they would continue working together to the "same ends." Mrs. Clark also mentioned that she was always willing to cooperate in courses of special training for pupils particularly gifted along certain lines.

label: text
text: A very pleasing programme of dances was then gone through, the rhythm and charm of movement of the performers greatly pleasing the audience:

text: Mr. Chan Kung-pok, by reason of his being engaged on General Chang Kai-ahek's staff at the Northern Front, will not be one of the Canton official delegates in the boycott negotiations. His place will be taken by Mr. Koo Mang-yue, who will act with Mr. Eugene Chen and Mr. T. V. Soong.—"Wah Tsz Yat Po."

label: text
text: Reports from Canton are that formal proceedings began yesterday at noon when credentials were exchanged.

label: text
text: It is expected that a full talk will be gone into to-day, so that detailed schemes may be presented to-morrow.

label: text
text: Reticence is being kept by official sources. There is a feeling of confidence and it is said that General Chang is of the view that he can leave for the Front in a week.

label: text
text: Owing to the difficulty in communications with Canton, news will necessarily be slow in getting through to Honglong. The best sign so far is the absence of any penministic rumours.

label: text
text: The inquiry into the death of a Chinese who was shot by a detective was resumed before Mr. R. E. Lindsell and a jury at the Central Magistracy to-day.

label: text
text: Evidence was given by the constable of firing four shots with the intention of stopping the man who escaped after discarding his coat. Previous to that the detective had carried out a search and found a dagger inside his clothing.

label: text
text: In his summing up to the jury, Mr. Lindsell said he saw no reason to doubt the evidence of the constable which was corroborated in all material particulars by other evidence. One very strong corroborating point was the evidence regarding the character of the deceased. No one had come forward to identify him.

label: text
text: Dealing with the use of 'fire-arms, Mr. Lindsell said that shoot-was permissible in certain cir-cumstances such as in chasing a man who is suspected of having committed a felony. If they be-

text: His Excellency has authorised a communique to the effect that Mr. Ku Many-yu has been appointed as one of the Canton Delegates in place of Mr. Chan Kung-pok; also that conference opened at noon yesterday when only formal business was transacted. The conference will resume to-day.

label: text
text: It is understood that Mr. Ku Mang-yu who was formerly Dean of the Peking University, is a Member of the Central Executive Committee of the Kwok Man Tong.

text: lieved the constable's story that the dagger was found on the man, then it was not an unreasonable assumption that the man was a felon, although the police had not been able to prove that a felony had been committed. The finding of the dagger gave rise to that suspicion. If the constable was unable to arrest the man by any other means, he was justified in firing to stop him. If further, in firing, he killed the man, then the killing was in law justifiable.

label: text
text: The following were the questions to the jury and their answers:—

label: text
text: Had the constable during the pursuit reasonable cause to suspect that the deceased had committed a felony? Yes.

label: text
text: If so, could he have effected an arrest by any other means short of firing? No.

label: text
text: Mr. Lindsell: On those answers I return a verdict of justifiable homicide.

text: "That was a smart piece of work," remarked Major C. Wilson at the Central Magistracy this morning when he was told that Mr. B. A. Hyder had caught a Chinese who was charged with the larceny of $20 from an old man at Des Voeux Road near the Wing On Company, yesterday forenoon.

label: text
text: It was stated by Inspector Spear that the defendant extracted the money from complainant's pocket and was seized by the owner. Defendant broke away by discarding the money and escaped in the direction of the Wing Lok Street wharf where he was caught.

label: text
text: Mr. Hyder's attention was drawn to the runaway by a whistle blown by the conductor a passing tram car. He said that he ran down a side lane leading into Connaught Road anticipating that the man would come that way and got him just in time.

text: Beyond the announcement of a delegate that "there have been developments." nothing has been officially divulged of to-day's meeting between the Trade Union Congress and the Miners' Executive, though Reuter learns that straight speaking on both sides cleared the air, whilst the Trade Union Congress promised the miners full support.—Reuter.

label: text
text: The Georgia State Banking Department announces that fifteen more Georgian Banks closed their doors to-day.

label: text
text: A temporary receivership had already been appointed for the Bankers Trust Company of Atlanta, whilst the Federal Judge heard a petition in bankruptcy proceedings to be brought against it by the Bank at Unatilla, Florida, which preferred certain charges. The State Banking Department, however, is of opinion that the situation is not so critical as it seems. The Banks concerned, mostly with a small capital of $20,000, are solvent. Their closing is in no way due to local conditions but to the embarrassment of the parent concern—the Bankers Trust Company.

label: text
text: According to experts the situation is a reflection of the recent failure in Florida caused directly or indirectly by the deflation of the land boom.—Reuter.

label: text
text: Flying from Paris to Omak in a 3,000 miles non-stop flight Captain Girler and Lieutenant d'Ordillet beaten the record of Captain Arrachart and his brother.—Reuter. [Paris cables of June 28 stated: The airmen brothers, Arrachart who departed from Paris, landed at Basrah after a 26 hours, 30 minutes non-stop flight. It is reported from Basra that Captain Arrachart and his brother, Sergeant Major Arrachart, in attempting to beat the record for a non-stop flight, left Labour at 5.30 a.m. yesterday and landed at Basrah, 2,734 miles distant, to day. They were in the air 20½ hours. The previous records was held by Captain Arrachart and Mr. Lemaître in February, 1925, when they flew 2,268 miles in 25 hours.]

label: text
text: Further evidence of a railway porter from Taipo and a woman occupier of a house at Second Street was called at the Central Magistracy this morning if the case in which a Chinese woman was charged with alleged kidnapping of an eleven-year old boy. Mr. E. S. C. Brooks appeared for the defence.

label: text
text: After hearing evidence, Mr. Lindsell considered that the charge could hardly be maintained, as the defendant had made no secret that the boy accompanied her on the train and in fact had told the principal tenant about it. He held that the boy accompanied the woman of his own accord and he did not believe the story that he was dragged into the train.

label: text
text: The defendant was discharged with a warning and the boy's brother, who was present in court, was ordered to look after him in future.

text: In the House of Commons, in reply to questions, Mr. S. Baldwin, Prime Minister, announced that the date of the Imperial Conference had been fixed for October 5. The agenda would include a general review of foreign policy and defence and questions arising therefrom, development systems, communications, and consultations between the Governments of the Empire on matters of common concern.

label: text
text: North Southwark) asked whether there would be an opportunity for the representation of Opposition opinion in view of the circumstances in South Africa, "Canada, and this country?

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin replied that the only difficulty was that the Imperial Conference had always been a conference of Governments, and no provision had been made for the official representation of Oppositions.—Reuter.
